notes: House of Al-Sabah is the ruling slot 23 (MD sprite) instead of MD slot 0; slot 0 holds Sheikh Sa'd al-Abdullah's Interior Ministry power bloc (1967 election rigging), slot 13 the Council of Ministers under Crown Prince Jaber al-Ahmad. Main opposition ANM (Ahmad al-Khatib) at 18; its PFLOAG-oriented Maoist youth at 19; NUKS students at 5. Islamists use real 1960s bodies: Social Reform Society (MB, 12), Social Cultural Society (Shia, 8), Da'wa cells (9), Abd al-Khaliq's Salafis (10). Ba'ath kept at 21 per MD.

0.name: Rijal al-Dakhiliyya
0.text:
The Interior Men are the security establishment built by Sheikh Sa'd al-Abdullah al-Salim al-Sabah, son of the late Emir Abdullah and Minister of Interior and Defence. They run the police, state security and the immigration and nationality offices, and the opposition accuses them of rigging the 1967 elections through ballot-stuffing and the mass naturalisation of loyal Bedouin voters.

They favour a firm hand: limits on the press and the National Assembly, deportation of troublesome expatriates, surveillance of Arab nationalists and close security ties with Britain and the West. Their leverage lies in the police, the electoral rolls and Sa'd's standing among the senior sheikhs of the ruling family.

1.name: Ghurfat Tijarat wa-Sina'at al-Kuwayt
1.english: Kuwait Chamber of Commerce and Industry
1.text:
The Kuwait Chamber of Commerce and Industry, founded in 1959, is the political home of the old merchant families who financed Kuwait before oil and helped shape the 1962 constitution with the ruling house. Its chairman, Abd al-Aziz Hamad al-Saqr, was the first Speaker of the National Assembly, and the leading merchant clans dominate its board.

The merchants defend constitutional government, property, Kuwaiti agency rights and a commercial, Western-oriented economy, while supporting Arab causes with discretion. They oppose both the Interior Ministry's heavy hand and the radicals' socialism. Their leverage lies in capital, the import trade, their diwaniyyas and their historic partnership with the Al-Sabah.

2.name: Jam'iyyat al-Khirrijin al-Kuwaytiyya
2.text:
The Kuwait Graduates Society was founded in 1964 by Kuwaitis returning from universities in Cairo, Beirut, Britain and the United States. Formally a professional association, it is the forum of the liberal intelligentsia: lawyers, doctors, engineers, senior civil servants and journalists who debate public affairs in its seminars and publications.

The Graduates champion the 1962 constitution, an independent judiciary, freedom of the press and assembly, women's education and political rights, and a civil service free of tribal and family favouritism. They admire Western democracies while backing Arab causes, and dislike both Interior Ministry repression and revolutionary dogma. Their leverage lies in expertise, the press and the growing educated middle class.

3.name: Al-Ittihad al-'Amm li-'Ummal al-Kuwayt
3.text:
The Kuwait Trade Union Federation was established in 1967 to unite the unions legalised by the 1964 labour law, above all the oil workers' unions of the Kuwait Oil Company and the government employees' associations. Only Kuwaiti citizens may hold office, so the federation speaks for a privileged minority of the workforce while the expatriate majority remains largely unorganised.

The unions demand higher wages, Kuwaitisation of skilled jobs, housing, pensions and a voice in the oil industry, and press for the gradual nationalisation of foreign oil interests. Moderate and nationalist in tone, they work with the Arab Nationalist deputies. Their leverage lies in the oil fields and the public sector.

4.name: Khalaya al-Ahmadi
4.text:
The Ahmadi Cells are the small communist circles of the oil town of Ahmadi and the industrial districts of Shuaiba and Fahaheel: Kuwaiti oil workers, schoolteachers and expatriate Iraqis, Iranians and Palestinians shaped by the Iraqi Communist Party and the Tudeh. With no legal party and under constant police watch, they meet in homes, union offices and night classes.

They follow Moscow's line: nationalisation of the Kuwait Oil Company, rights for citizen and expatriate workers alike, equal citizenship and alliance with the Soviet Union against imperialism. They see the Arab Nationalists as petty-bourgeois allies. Their leverage lies in the oil installations and the large, voiceless expatriate workforce.

5.name: Al-Ittihad al-Watani li-Talabat al-Kuwayt
5.text:
The National Union of Kuwaiti Students was founded in 1964 and has branches at the new Kuwait University and among Kuwaitis studying in Cairo, Beirut, Britain and the United States. Since the 1967 defeat its congresses have been dominated by the radical left of the Arab Nationalist Movement, and its branches abroad are among the loudest voices of Gulf youth.

The Union calls for solidarity with the fedayeen and the Dhofar revolution, the nationalisation of oil, an end to Western bases in the Gulf, academic freedom and a democracy without princely privilege. It denounces American imperialism and the conservative monarchies. Its leverage lies in student mobilisation, street protest and its hold on the future Kuwaiti elite.

6.name: Ansar al-Fida'iyyin
6.text:
The Friends of the Fedayeen are the Kuwaitis who give money, shelter and sometimes their own service to the Palestinian guerrillas: merchants who fund Fatah, mosque committees that collect for the martyrs, and young men who volunteer in the camps of Jordan. Their most prominent figure is Sheikh Fahd al-Ahmad al-Jaber al-Sabah, brother of the Crown Prince, who has volunteered with Fatah.

They are pious, patriotic and hostile to the West, demanding that Kuwait place its oil wealth and diplomacy at the service of the war against Israel and its American protector. Indifferent to socialism, they mix Islamic sentiment with Arab honour. Their leverage lies in money, royal patronage and Kuwait's large Palestinian community.

7.name: Dubbat al-Qanat
7.text:
The Officers of the Canal are the Kuwaiti officers and soldiers of the contingent that Kuwait sent to the Egyptian front after the June War. Serving beside Egyptian units on the Suez Canal during the War of Attrition, they have come under Israeli fire and absorbed the political culture of Nasser's army.

Back home they compare Kuwait's small dynastic army, its British advisers and its favouritism unfavourably with Egypt's revolutionary officer corps. They want a stronger, Arab-nationalist military, compulsory service, a break with Western defence ties and an army that answers to the nation rather than to the sheikhs. Their leverage lies in combat prestige and in the barracks.

8.name: Jam'iyyat al-Thaqafa al-Ijtima'iyya
8.text:
The Social Cultural Society is the leading association of Kuwait's Shia, founded in the 1960s by merchants, clerics and educated young men of a community that forms a substantial minority of the citizenry. It runs lectures, libraries, charities and religious celebrations and serves as the meeting place of Shia deputies and notables.

The Society favours religious education, Shia representation in the Assembly and the civil service, freedom for husayniyyas and Ja'fari family courts, and loyalty to the Al-Sabah, who have long relied on Shia merchants against the Sunni opposition. Its outlook is reformist and moderate, drawing on the teaching of Najaf. Its leverage lies in merchant wealth, communal solidarity and its usefulness to the ruling house.

9.name: Hizb al-Da'wa al-Islamiyya
9.text:
The Islamic Da'wa Party, founded in Najaf in the late 1950s around Ayatollah Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr, has a discreet following in Kuwait among Shia students, teachers and young clerics with family ties to Iraq and Iran. Since the Ba'athist regime in Baghdad began persecuting the Najaf clergy in 1969, Kuwait has become a refuge and relay for its activists.

The party seeks an Islamic state built on Sadr's critique of both capitalism and communism and guided by qualified jurists. It rejects Western influence and Soviet atheism, and regards the Gulf monarchies as illegitimate. Its leverage lies in secret cells, mosque and husayniyya networks, and the revolutionary energy of a generation of young Shia.

10.name: Al-Jama'a al-Salafiyya
10.text:
The Salafi Group is the circle of Kuwaiti and expatriate students gathered around Sheikh Abd al-Rahman Abd al-Khaliq, an Egyptian-born graduate of the Islamic University of Medina who settled in Kuwait in the mid-1960s. Meeting in mosques and homes, it teaches strict adherence to the Qur'an, the Sunna and the pious ancestors, free of Sufi and sectarian accretions.

The Salafis stay out of opposition politics, owe obedience to the Emir as lawful ruler and look to the Saudi ulama for guidance. They campaign for public morality, Islamic education and the Shari'a as the source of legislation, and reject both nationalism and the Brotherhood's activism. Their leverage lies in Saudi goodwill and growing student piety.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani, maintains secret cells in Kuwait among Palestinian and Jordanian teachers, clerks and engineers and a handful of Kuwaiti students. Banned and closely watched by state security, its members distribute leaflets and hold study circles in private homes.

The party rejects the Gulf emirates, the Arab republics and the very idea of nationalism, preaching that only a restored caliphate uniting all Muslims can free Palestine and end Western domination. It shuns elections and guerrilla war alike, seeking power through army officers. Its leverage is limited but steady: ideological discipline among the educated expatriates who staff Kuwait's schools.

12.name: Jam'iyyat al-Islah al-Ijtima'i
12.text:
The Social Reform Society, founded in 1963 as successor to the Islamic Guidance Society of the early 1950s, is the public face of the Muslim Brotherhood in Kuwait. It is led by Abdullah al-Ali al-Mutawa, a respected merchant, and draws teachers, civil servants and students into its charities, Qur'an circles and summer camps.

The Society calls for the Shari'a as the main source of legislation, Islamic education and public morality, and wants Kuwait to champion Muslim causes abroad, above all Palestine. It avoids confrontation with the ruling family and treats the Arab Nationalists as its main rivals. Its leverage lies in charity networks, merchant donations and a growing student following.

13.name: Majlis al-Wuzara'
13.text:
The Council of Ministers is the government of Kuwait, led since 1965 by Prime Minister and, since 1966, Crown Prince Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Jaber al-Sabah. Senior sheikhs hold the sovereign ministries, among them Foreign Minister Sabah al-Ahmad, while commoner technocrats such as Finance and Oil Minister Abd al-Rahman al-Atiqi run the economic portfolios.

The Council governs a cautious, paternalist welfare state: free housing, schooling and health care, public jobs for citizens and generous aid to Arab states through the Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development. Abroad it follows non-alignment, keeping relations with both Washington and Moscow and funding the PLO. Its leverage is total control of oil revenues and the civil service.

14.name: Kutlat al-Qaba'il
14.text:
The Tribal Bloc is the group of Bedouin deputies and sheikhs from the 'Awazim, 'Ajman, Mutayr, Rashayida and 'Anaza who dominate the outer constituencies around Ahmadi and Jahra. Their tribesmen have been naturalised in large numbers through the 1960s, settled in new housing areas and recruited into the army and police.

They are loyal to the Emir and the government, conservative in religion and custom, and indifferent to the ideological battles of the town. In return for their votes they expect citizenship for kinsmen, housing, jobs and services. Their leverage lies in numbers, in the armed forces and in the government's need for a counterweight to the urban opposition.

15.name: Bank al-Kuwayt al-Watani
15.text:
The National Bank of Kuwait was founded in 1952 by a group of leading merchants as the first locally owned bank in the Gulf, ending the monopoly of British banking. Its founders and board read like a roll of the old merchant elite, the Saqr, Ghanim, Kharafi and Hamad families among them, and it finances the import trade and the construction boom.

The bank stands for private capital, a stable currency, the merchants' share of oil wealth through state contracts and land purchases, and cooperation with Western finance. It prefers quiet influence over the Emir and his ministers to street politics. Its leverage lies in credit, deposits and the merchant class's grip on Kuwait's private economy.

16.name: Tujjar al-Suq
16.text:
The Merchants of the Souq are the shopkeepers, money changers, gold dealers and small importers of Kuwait's old market quarter, many from families who once traded with India, Basra and East Africa. Overshadowed by the great merchant houses and the state, they gather in the souq's coffee houses and in their own diwaniyyas.

They want Kuwait to remain a free port: low customs duties, light licensing, no price controls and no state monopolies, together with protection against foreign competitors and expatriate traders. They distrust socialist planning and princely business ventures alike. Their leverage lies in numbers, their role in daily commerce and the votes they carry in the old town districts.

17.name: Ahl al-Bahr
17.text:
The People of the Sea are the last pearl divers, ship captains, dhow builders and fishermen of Kuwait, whose way of life collapsed with the pearl trade and the coming of oil. Gathered in the coastal quarters and diwaniyyas of Sharq and Jibla, they watch oil slicks, refinery waste and land reclamation spoil Kuwait Bay and its fishing grounds.

They call for protecting the bay, the fish stocks and the shoreline from pollution and unchecked building, preserving maritime heritage and curbing gas flaring and industrial dumping. Nostalgic, conservative and loyal to the ruling family, they have no party, but their elders are respected as guardians of Kuwait's pre-oil identity, which is their only real leverage.

18.name: Harakat al-Qawmiyyin al-'Arab
18.text:
The Arab Nationalist Movement is Kuwait's main opposition, led by Dr. Ahmad al-Khatib, deputy speaker of the first National Assembly, and Jasim al-Qatami. Organised around the Independence Club, the weekly al-Tali'a and the teachers' and students' unions, its candidates were largely kept out of the Assembly by the rigged 1967 elections, and its radical youth is pulling toward Marxism.

Khatib's nationalists demand a genuine parliamentary democracy, freedom of the press and association, Kuwaiti control of oil and a fairer distribution of its wealth, Arab unity and support for the fedayeen. They are non-aligned, friendly to Nasser and critical of the Western oil companies. Their leverage lies in the educated middle class and Arab public opinion.

19.name: Ansar Zufar
19.text:
The Friends of Dhofar are young Kuwaiti radicals, many of them former Arab Nationalist Movement members, who have broken with Ahmad al-Khatib's reformism and rallied to the Popular Front for the Liberation of the Occupied Arabian Gulf, the Maoist-inspired guerrilla movement fighting in Oman's Dhofar province. They collect money, print leaflets and send volunteers and supplies toward Aden.

They see the Gulf monarchies as creations of British imperialism and call for a people's war across the peninsula, inspired by China and Vietnam rather than Moscow. They reject parliamentary politics as an illusion. Their leverage lies in student and teacher networks and their links to the revolutionary regime in Aden.

20.name: Ahl al-Sur
20.text:
The People of the Wall are the 'original' Kuwaitis, descendants of families settled in the town by 1920, the year its last wall was built, who hold first-class citizenship under the 1959 nationality law. They are already a minority in their own country, outnumbered by Arab and Asian expatriates and by newly naturalised Bedouin.

Their populism is defensive: guarantee jobs, housing and land for true Kuwaitis, restrict naturalisation and the expatriate presence, keep the vote for original citizens and resist Palestinian, Egyptian and Iraqi influence in schools and ministries. They distrust both pan-Arab radicals and the government's tribal clients. Their leverage lies in their status, their diwaniyyas and their grip on the electoral register.

21.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-'Arabi al-Ishtiraki
21.text:
The Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party has had a clandestine Kuwaiti organisation since the 1950s, recruited among teachers, students and Iraqi, Syrian and Palestinian expatriates. Split since 1966 between the Damascus and Baghdad commands, many of its members now look to the Iraqi regime of Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr, whose troops have been stationed on Kuwaiti soil near Umm Qasr since 1969.

The Ba'athists call for Arab unity under a single revolutionary party, the end of dynastic rule, nationalisation of oil and the sharing of Gulf wealth with the Arab nation. Militaristic and conspiratorial, they are hostile to the West and to Kuwaiti particularism. Their leverage lies in Iraqi power next door and in expatriate cells.

22.name: Al-Quwwat al-Musallaha al-Kuwaytiyya
22.text:
The Kuwait Armed Forces were built up after independence in 1961, when Iraq's claim to the emirate brought British troops back to defend it. Under Defence Minister Sheikh Sa'd al-Abdullah they comprise a small army, an air force flying British Lightnings and Hunters, and a contingent on the Egyptian front. Senior commands are reserved for sheikhs and trusted families.

The officer corps is loyal, well paid and British-trained, and sees itself as the guardian of independence against Iraqi ambitions. Its senior men prefer order and close Western ties, though younger officers absorb Arab nationalism. Its leverage lies in being the only armed force able to defend, or to seize, the state.

23.name: Al Sabah
23.text:
The House of Al-Sabah has ruled Kuwait since the mid-eighteenth century, when the Bani Utub chose Sabah I as their sheikh. Emir Sabah al-Salim al-Sabah has reigned since 1965, succeeding his brother Abdullah, father of independence and of the 1962 constitution; power alternates between the Al-Jaber and Al-Salim branches, and Jaber al-Ahmad is Crown Prince.

The dynasty rules a constitutional emirate in which the Emir appoints the government, shares legislation with an elected National Assembly and distributes oil wealth through a generous welfare state. It balances merchants, tribes, Shia and nationalists at home, and Iraq, Iran and Saudi Arabia abroad. Its leverage is oil, legitimacy and the loyalty of the security forces.
